articles.title: A Note on How Jevons and YBMD Indices Differ According to Price Relative Concentration
articles.abstract: Most national statistical offices employ the Jevons index to measure the Consumer Price Index (CPI) at the elementary aggregation level. From an axiomatic perspective, it is also considered the most appropriate unweighted price index. The YBMD index has some attractive properties compared with the Jevons index. By exploiting a factorization of the YBMD index, this note demonstrates that the two indices differ according to the concentration of price relatives between the base and current periods.

articles.title: Trends in Labour Force Survey Response Rates and Components of Nonresponse Bias: Evidence from the 2003 to 2023 Icelandic LFS
articles.authors: Hafsteinn Einarsson, Joseph W. Sakshaug, Arndís Vilhjálmsdóttir, Ólafur Már Sigurðsson
articles.abstract: Response rates in labour force surveys have declined over time in many countries, posing risks to the quality of the collected data. Comprehensive analyses of trends in participation and respondent composition are therefore important for evaluating labour force data quality. In this article, we analyse cross-sectional response rate and nonresponse bias trends over a period of twenty-one years (2003–2023) in the Icelandic Labour Force Survey (IS-LFS), a quarterly telephone survey of individuals. Specifically, we decompose nonresponse into three parts: (1) unfielded noncontacts that lack a known telephone number, (2) fielded noncontacts that have a known telephone number, and (3) refusals, and evaluate their relative contributions to response rate and nonresponse bias trends. Our results show that response rates have declined from 81.5 percent in 2003 to 49.7 percent in 2023, averaging 1.5 percentage points per year, while the average absolute relative nonresponse bias (unweighted) more than doubled over the same period. These trends are primarily driven by noncontacts (fielded and unfielded) rather than refusals, particularly since 2013. In recent years, having an immigration background has been the strongest predictor of nonresponse, followed by age and education. Individuals not in the labour force are consistently less likely to participate relative to employed persons. The IS-LFS overestimates the share of the population that is employed by 5.6 percentage points on average relative to register benchmarks, which is reduced to 3.8 percentage points by weighting. We conclude with a discussion of the practical implications of these findings for labour force surveys and sample surveys more generally.

Mass Perceptions of Agency Ideology
articles.authors: Maxwell B Allamong, Manuel P Teodoro
articles.abstract: Federal agencies have become central actors in contemporary American politics, overseeing salient policy domains with clear ideological stakes. While scholars have long considered ideology as an important dimension of bureaucratic reputation, existing measures have largely relied on surveys of political elites or indicators such as employees’ campaign donations, leaving mass perceptions unexplored. Using data from a team module on the 2022 Cooperative Election Study, we provide descriptive evidence of the public’s perceptions of the ideological leanings of twelve federal agencies. We show that the public perceives meaningful ideological variation across agencies, with some seen as relatively more liberal (EPA), some more conservative (DOD), and others ideologically moderate (USPS). Additionally, mass perceptions of ideology closely align with measures derived from expert assessments, agency employees, or advanced computational approaches. They also correlate with partisanship, with Republicans (Democrats) rating agencies as relatively more liberal (conservative). Together, these findings establish ideology as a broadly perceptible, if partially variable, feature of government agencies, with potential to shape how citizens evaluate and interact with the American bureaucracy.

articles.title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
articles.authors: Edgar Cook, James Martherus, Alexander Podkul, Anja Kilibarda
articles.abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.
